newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian PM calls for unity in Yeltsin absence.
newsitem.headline: Russian PM calls for unity in Yeltsin absence.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, facing prolonged uncertainty after doctors delayed President Boris Yeltsin's heart surgery, on Thursday called for cabinet unity in the president's absence.
Focusing on a looming battle with parliament over next year's budget, Chernomyrdin told a cabinet meeting he would not stand for ministers bickering or lobbying in parliament for extra cash.

"If members of the government start playing any kind of game there, in the State Duma (lower house of parliament), I warn them that whoever they are, whatever their rank, they will not work here," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.

His brusque words were aimed at ensuring unity in the ranks in a prolonged period of political uncertainty as Yeltsin awaits a heart bypass operation. The delay could increase the risk of political infighting and jostling for power.

Chernomyrdin's comments represented a warning to his colleagues not to follow security tsar Alexander Lebed down the path of outspoken criticism to defend their own interests and increase their profile.
But he held out an olive branch to Lebed, widely seen as his main power rival, by saying defence spending should be reviewed because the ministry had not had a fair hearing.
"The defence ministry had not been listened to at all," Interfax quoted the 58-year-old prime minsiter as saying.

Lebed wrote to Yeltsin and Chernomyrdin last month to demand more spending on defence in the budget, which needs the approval of the opposition-dominated Duma. He said in an interview published on Wednesday there was a danger of an army mutiny.

Chernomyrdin, who has taken a relatively low profile in Yeltsin's absence since the end of June, appeared unusually assertive the day after a team of doctors said Yeltsin should not be operated on for at least six more weeks.

The doctors said the 65-year-old president had a good chance of a full recovery, but he would be likely to need about two months to recuperate after the operation -- grafting in veins from the leg to bypass clogged heart arteries.
That leaves plenty of scope for more of the jostling for position in the Kremlin which political analysts say has intensified since Yeltsin fell ill.
Lebed has made controversial statements in the last few days which have highlighted his tendency to step out of line with others in Russia's leadership.

He provided a glimpse of the infighting which appears to have isolated him in the Kremlin in an interview published in Izvestia newspaper on Thursday, although he issued a statement distancing himself from the comments.
"He (Yeltsin) communicates with a limited circle of people of which I am not a part," Lebed told Izvestia.
He said some of the politicians who have followed liberal Western recipes for Kremlin reforms as "yesterday's men" and made surpisingly conciliatory comments about the communists.
Lebed also raised eyebrows in Washington with comments published in the newspaper Vechernyaya Moskva on Wednesday condemning U.S. missile attacks on Iraq this month.
He told Vechernyaya Moskva that if that happened to Russia: "I would hit back instantly. With everything we've got."
